meta.framing: How did researchers weigh the historical, artistic, and radiocarbon evidence to settle whether the Shroud of Turin is a first-century burial cloth or a medieval creation?

response:
The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing the faint front and back image of a man, and the question of its origin has long turned on whether that image belongs to a first-century tomb or a fourteenth-century workshop. Because the cloth carries so arresting a figure, its documentary trail begins with public display: the earliest secure historical record of the shroud places it in Lirey, France, in the 1350s, when the de Charny family exhibited it in their collegiate church. Historians have treated this Lirey appearance as the starting point against which every later claim must be measured, since no reliable text locates the cloth anywhere earlier.

The Lirey exhibitions of the 1350s predate by roughly three decades the memorandum that Bishop Pierre d'Arcis wrote in 1389, in which he claimed that an artist had confessed to painting the cloth. That memorandum indicates the grounds on which Antipope Clement VII ruled in 1390 that the cloth could be exhibited only as a representation and not as the true burial shroud; the bishop's accusation of artistic fabrication is precisely the concern the papal restriction answers. The object's subsequent history added physical complications. The shroud was damaged by a fire in 1532; in other words, the 1532 fire that damaged it took place in Turin Cathedral, and the scorch marks and patches from that blaze remain visible on the linen today, complicating any physical examination of the fabric.

Scientific testing eventually supplied a direct measurement. Three laboratories, at Oxford, Zurich, and the University of Arizona, radiocarbon-dated samples of the shroud in 1988. The British Museum performed the radiocarbon measurements on the shroud, serving as the institutional anchor of the project rather than as one of the three dating centres named in its protocol. The resulting figures were pooled and subjected to statistical analysis before publication.

The radiocarbon study published in Nature in 1989 concluded that the shroud's linen dates to AD 1260–1390, even though the 1988 radiocarbon samples were all cut from a single corner of the cloth. The Nature authors, reviewing the sampling question, determined that the single-corner sample was representative of the whole cloth, so that the AD 1260–1390 date holds for the entire textile. That sampling choice has shaped the subsequent debate, because a single location cannot by itself establish that it represents the whole textile. Critics and defenders alike have therefore framed the medieval reading of the date in terms of what the measured threads actually were. At least one of the following holds, perhaps both: the flax for the shroud's linen was harvested in the medieval period, or the corner from which the radiocarbon sample was cut contains medieval repair threads. Chemical and microscopic studies of the reserve material have been invoked on both sides of that question, and neither line of analysis has excluded the other.

Whatever the radiocarbon date says about the linen, the image raises a distinct problem, and here the evidence divides sharply. The date of AD 1260–1390 concerns when the fibres grew. The question of the figure admits exactly two answers, one of which must be true: either the image on the shroud was created by a medieval artisan, or the image on the shroud was not created by a medieval artisan. Proponents of the first account point to the d'Arcis testimony and to the coincidence between the radiocarbon range and the cloth's first documented appearance; proponents of the second stress that no pigment-based technique has convincingly reproduced the image's superficial, negative-like character.

Institutional caution has accompanied this scholarly division. The Catholic Church has never officially declared the shroud to be authentic; that is, the Vatican has made no formal pronouncement affirming the shroud as the burial cloth of Jesus. Popes have permitted veneration of the cloth as an icon of the Passion, which leaves the historical and scientific questions to researchers rather than to doctrine.
